Within the next two weeks strong
efforts will be made by the manage
ment of the Normal school at Weston
to secure the guarantee of sufficient
funds to maintain the school until
the next session of the legislature,
and those in charge are confident that
they will succeed.


A meeting of the board of regents

fices of Carter, Raley & Raley, and
the following members were present:
r. Alexander, president; P. A. Worth

Stone. Also, President French was
in attendance to advise with the re-

the prospect for continuing the school
President French, P. A. Worthington
and G. W. Proebstel were appointed
as a committee to solicit funds for
the school, and directed to report at
apother meeting to be held on June
80, at which time definite action re-
garding the future of the school win
be taken.

had no doubt whatever but that suf-

tinue the school with its full faculty
during the next two years, or rather
until the next session of the legisla-
ture. A large proportion Of the
amount will be raised by the people
of Weston, and he stated that assur-
ances of support have also been made
by numerous people in other parts Of
the county.


According to President French
money will be solicited as a loan
rather than as a donation. for II Is
fully expected that the legislature
can be induced to reimburse sub
scribers for the amounts given, should
the school be maintained during the
interval. In fact the strength dis
played by the friends of the normal
schools at the last session is regarded
as almost positive guarantee that such
will be done.


AS to Just how much will be re-
quired to keep the school going until
an appropriation can be secured, Pres
ident French could not definitely say,
hut intimated that $4,000 would be
sufficient. 1t is the desire to run the
school with the entire faculty, and
thus avoid impairing the usefulness
of the school.

Evans, commanding officer of the North Atlantic fleet; Admiral Sands, superintendent of the Naval Academy, and Governor Warfield of Maryland. John Crees, about thirty years of age,
resident Of Grand River, lying in the
county Jail awaiting the next term of
the district court to answer to the
charge of breaking and entering the de-
pot at Grand River and taking liquor
therefrom, escaped from the Jail some
time Sunday night and remains at liber-
ty.


The manner in which he effected his
escape was told by Walter Rockhold,
another prisoner who is serving fif-
teen day sentence for larceny. In some
way Crees secured a wire stove poker
and with the same managed to slide the
two bars locking the door of his cell
and then made his way to the top of the
cage. He then tore hole through the
ceiling and climbed into the garret.
With the stove poker still his only tool
he began work upon the brick wall and
soon dug enough bricks from their place
to enable him to squeeze through. Hav-
ing completed the means of escape he
tied two blankets together, fastened
one end inside, and by their aid let him
self through the opening to the ground.


The escape of Crees was discovered
about 6 o'clock Monday morning by
Sheriff Wallace who had just arisen and
in passing around the north side of the
Jail found the blankets hanging from
the Jagged hole in the north wall. The
authorities in all surrounding towns
were Immediately notified and every
effort made to recapture the fugitive
but as we go to press he had not been
located.


A heavy rain was falling Sunday even
Ing and throughout the night which
fact greatly served the purpose of
Crees. Few persons were on the street
even in the early evening and the roar
OF the storm prevented any noise made
by the prisoner being heard by Sheriff
Wallace.


The crime of which he stood charged
was committed on or about August 4th.
He was arrested and taken before Jus
tice John Durham at Grand River. He
acknowledged his guilt and offered to
settle for the liquor secured. Justice
Durham bound the prisoner over to the
district court and he was brought to
Leon Wednesday, August 9th, by Con-
stable Robert Brammer and placed in
the county Jail to await trial.

The first death occurred at 11:15 o'clock P. M. on the Chesapeake & Ohio railway yard, at the foot of Huntington avenue, where Earl Gilchrist was at work on pole, cutting down dead wires. A negro helper, who was on the ground below, was the only eyewitness to the tragedy. It seems that the lineman had cut four dead wires and was holding them in his hands. In some way the wires surged and came in contact with an electric live feed wire, carrying something over 1000 volts of electricity.

Hung By Life-Belt

Having no climbers, the negro was unable to go to the assistance of the stricken man and without waste of time he ran off and brought back Ed. C. Pleasant and A. L. Phillips, two other linemen who were at work in another part of the city. These men mounted the pole and lowered the body of their comrade to the ground. Life was extinct and the clothing was in flames.

Life Was Extinct.

The body was carried in the general hospital with all possible haste, the linemen hoping that spark of life might be left. At the hospital, however, the body was pronounced dead and it was stated that death must have been instantaneous.

Dr. B. H. Gary was summoned and an inquest held. On the Jury were Floyd Smith, R. A. Fowler, H. H. Brushwood, W. R. Ballard, L. H. Fraser and J. A. Bragg.

After hearing several witnesses, the Jury rendered the following verdict: We, the Jury, find that the deceased came to his death by an electric shock while in the employ of the Southern Bell Telephone Company as a lineman.

Before this inquest was over, the coroner was notified of the death of Ashby Harris. In keeping the Jury together, he proceeded to the scene of the second tragedy.

Gilchrist was native Lynchburg, where he was employed by the Southern Bell Telephone Company until he came here several months ago. J. of Lynchburg, and belonged to the local electrical workers union.

The deceased is survived by his parents, Mr. and Mrs. John H. Gilchrist, of Lynchburg, five brothers and three sisters: G. H., Walter W., Raymond and James Gilchrist, and Misses Eleanor, Ida and Frances Gilchrist.

The body will be shipped to Lynchburg today for interment. Mr. Edward Gilchrist, VIII, lives in Norfolk, came over to this city last night and will accompany the body to Lynchburg.

Manganese is added to the glass to neutralize the green color which is caused by the presence of ferrous iron, and in the course of time, this manganese changes from its colorless state, and, turning violet, gives its hue to the old glass. A striking confirmation of this is afforded by the fact that the most rapid coloring has been observed at high elevations in tropical regions. book. It happened to be of the same
color as her kimono, which was also
pretty. Attached to her book was a
tiny little electric light, with shade.
The battery lay by her side.


The husband reseated himself at the
center table. By his side was an open
book with a paper knife keeping the
place for him. It was under the read-
ing lamp.


"How long have you been married
now?" asked the woman as she took
her seat in a big armchair.


"About six months," said they, smiling
simultaneously.


The woman, who had just come from
a gay dinner party where she had
laughed for two hours with a lot of
friends, glanced quickly from one to
the other, taking in the books, the
lamps, their attitudes of repose, the
quiet of the room, the air of having fin-
ished with fun altogether.


"I see," said she. "I know how it is.
I used to be married, read then, and
read and read. I nearly put my eyes
out reading. I read sometimes till 8
o'clock in the morning and after."


"I do that now," smiled the wife.


"Really," went on the woman. "I think there wasn't a book that came
out then I didn't read, devoured
them omnivorously."


"And now?" said they.


The woman smiled serenely at them
from the recess of her big armchair.


"Now," said she, "I never read since
the books that's on the market. I don't
know what's come out, and I don't
care. I go by bookstands from one
year's end to the other and never think
of them."


"Why?" asked they.


"I'm no longer married," explained
the woman. "I no longer vegetate and
read and read and vegetate. I live
now," she added.—New York Press.

Special to The Times-Dispatch.

COLUMBIA, S. C., April 27.—The second day's session of the Conference for Education in the South was distinguished by a series of notable addresses and by an attendance rarely equalled in a public meeting here.

An overflow audience of cultured citizens and visitors was present at the session tonight. President Ogden occupied the chair, using a gavel sent by a Virginia lady. Superintendent Phillips, of the Birmingham city schools, read a valuable paper on the high school in the public schools of the South.

He was followed by Superintendent Hand, of the Chester, S. C., schools, who presented a striking array of arguments in support of compulsory education and surprising evidence of the growing popularity in the South of the principle. Ex-Mayor of New York, Seth Low, closed the regular programme in lucid discussion on the history of public education in New York, citing the many phases of its advancement and its periods of regressive decline consequent upon political corruption or partisan upheavals.

The programme was broken by a lady from New York, who taught the Indians for seven years. She made an eloquent plea for the "Original American" and rendered some of their war and love songs with delightful effect.

In the morning there was a notable gathering of South Carolina College, when inspiring short addresses were made by President Ogden, Mr. Low, Dr. McKelway and Dr. Alderman, and in the afternoon a reception was given members of the conference on the campus by the students and faculty. The morning session of the conference was given over to superintendents of public instruction from eleven Southern States. Reports from them all indicated remarkable growth in educational work.

The Morning Session.

The morning session of the conference was given up to the conference of Southern State superintendents of education, this being one of the features of the big meeting. The most interesting feature of the morning was the rather impromptu symposium in the chapel of the South Carolina College at 9:45 o'clock, the speakers being Robert C. Ogden, Hon. Seth Low, Prof. St. Clair McKelway, and Dr. F. A. Alderman.

The students of the college were gathered in the chapel for the regular morning exercises, which were varied by these addresses. Mr. Ogden said that although he was the president of an educational movement, yet he was remarkably ignorant, for his life had been lived in a prosaic occupation, and he was only a plain American business man. That there was a growing demand for educated men in the business world, he had no doubt, as no work is so well done that if it cannot be done better, and in the contact with other people, it was even more valuable, for the world demands intelligent and well informed men in every line of business. Mr. Ogden called special attention to the common fallacy that modern college education did not aid a man to go into the business world. In his opinion the fact that education generally tended towards idealism and common sense carried into any business in the world would accomplish much.

Low and McKelway.

Mr. Ogden was followed by the Hon. Seth Low, who spoke upon the attitude which young men should have towards the various public questions of the day. It is too often the case, he said, that men form their ideas of things and then go to work to find the facts which sustain those theories, ignoring those that are not in accord with them. He advised the young men to get first their facts and base their ideas upon these. Mr. Low referred to the time when he was president of Columbia University, and said that the connection of that university with the South Carolina College. He laid special stress on the importance of education as it generally produces wideness and breadth of thought. These qualities, he said, were commendable in all walks of life and were responsible for much of the work of to-day.

A Brooklyn Eagle, then addressed the students and in his usual deliberate manner speaking, made a profound impression on his audience. He said that he was besides a journalist, a member of the State Board of Regents of New York, and that he was deeply interested now in the correlation of the schools of the South. He said that the State University of South Carolina should be, as Alexander Hamilton, who planned Columbia University, should be, in New York, the center around which clustered all the other schools.

Dr. Alderman Speaks.

Dr. Alderman, president of the University of Virginia, was the next speaker and the last. He made a speech which was received with unusually prolonged applause and among other things he said that he had recently read an excellent article in the Atlantic Monthly on "Difficulties and Dangers of a College President." Some time, he said, he wanted to write or get some one else to write an article on the pleasures of a college president. He spoke of the type of student in the South and said that he was more serious minded than the students of other sections of the country.

A Hartman official gave out the information yesterday that commencing Jan. 1, the new train which is intended to quicken the mail schedule between Ogden and the coast will be put on and will lessen the time now used by about five hours. It will also mean the saving of a working day in the delivery of the mail at the coast end.

The new train will be No. 9 going west and No. 10 eastbound. At the present time No. 2, the fast mail on the Union Pacific, arrives in Ogden at 4 o'clock in the afternoon, and the mail brought here on that train goes west on No. 9 fifty five minutes later, with the new schedule clock and will pull out for the west five minutes later. The intention now is to make the new train for the carrying of mail only, hence aside from the division stops for changing engines and the water stops, there will be no scheduled stops for the train between here and the coast.

The scheduled time will be on an average of forty miles per hour, and instead of the mail arriving in San Francisco at 8 o'clock as at present, it will reach the coast at 2 o'clock noon, in season for an afternoon delivery. It is expected that this schedule will be much better than the present one, and so much quicker than that established by the Santa Fe that there will be no question as to the Hartman roads holding the contract for the carrying of the transcontinental mails on the next reweighing. Over three hours will be deducted from the present time between Ogden and Sparks alone and the time for the rest of the run is equally as much improved. Eastbound the train will reach Ogden at 6 o'clock, and the mail will go east on Union Pacific No. 8 an hour later.

The original arrangement was to have the mail train run through Ogden in the morning, but at the conference at Salt Lake Saturday this was seen to be impracticable and the decision was reached to make the schedule the same as given above.

It is stated that there was no reference made to the new Los Angeles limited or Overland limited trains, and their schedules will remain the same on the new timetable as at present. It is taken, therefore, that the mail service is the only one with which they are dealing at the present time and if the new schedule will be sufficient to secure the next mail contract for the Hartman lines it will have served the purpose for which it was intended.

stage in the famous Gaynor and Greene
case was completed when Justice Davidson
to-day dismissed the fugitives' application

Lafontaine, on the ground that his appointment by the Dominion Government and not

of extradition treaties belongs in a marked

the question of its constitutionality had

counsel announced that an appeal would
be taken from Justice Davidson's decision,

ginia expends every year a great amount

San Juan county and the tedious, dusty
ride from Durango into the valley of
Animas is thing of the past.

Many rumors are current as to the
future plans of the new railroad, but
nothing absolutely authentic can be
learned. It is said that the track lay-
ers will be sent back up the line
from Aztec to level and make the
track fit for trains that box cars
will be at once placed by the track.
Here for a temporary depot and the
construction work toward Farming-
ton will continue in ten days. No def-
inite authority will verify the above.

The grading will be completed into
Pennington by September, but it is
very doubtful if the rails will reach
there before October. The chances
for the railroad company carrying pas-
sengers in time for the fair in
September, 10, 20 and 31 are de-
cidedly adverse, but promise of ex-
cursions for the Aztec fair September
10, 20 and 31 has been made and will
be fulfilled without doubt.

No construction work beyond Farm-
ington will be done apparently, as the
grading contractors are moving away
as soon as they complete their con-
tracts. The legal difficulties which
the Rio Grande is having with the Ar-
izona & Colorado railroad company
over right of way between Farming-
ton and Aztec is also said to cause
a suspension of track laying beyond
this point at present.

The side tracks at the depot site in
Aztec are in and the plans for a very
nice depot have been drawn. Aztec
and Pennington will get similar depot
buildings. The depot site here is lo-
cated just above the big ditch on land
owned by Col. W. H. Williams. The
railroad to the Rio Grande will be
aided by enterprising citizens of Aztec, who
raised $1,000 for the purpose. The
depot will be about five blocks from
the center of the town and will over-
look the beautiful orchards and pro-
ductive fields that surround Aztec, the
most fertile land in all the Animas
valley. The railroad company plans
a reservoir to pipe water for engine
and depot. They have made state-
ment that if the town will put in wat-
er mains the railroad will do its share
toward putting in a pumping station
and large reservoir on the hills back
of the depot. The matter is now under
advisement and if the company
decides to go ahead the progressive
citizens of Aztec will do their share.
It is fully realized here that to make
a city of homes the comforts of a
home must be made possible, and ev-
ery effort looking to this end will re-
ceive the support of Aztec.

Preparations for the San Juan coun-
ty fair and carnival will now go ahead
with renewed zeal under the stimu-
lus of the new road's arrival. Sep-
tember 10, 20 and 31 have been set
aside for the dates and big exhibit
of fruit, grain, vegetables, coal, culin-
ary products, etc., is being prepared.
Durango's fair takes place the week
following and a number of exhibitors
may be induced to take their displays
to that point.

A rousing welcome has been accord-
ed the new railroad and now if the
Rio Grande will give this country the
right schedule of trains, a feeling that
the Animas valley is in touch with
the outside world will put the last
drop in the cup of happiness of the
people of San Juan county, New Mex-
ico.

London, Jan. 21.--The Express correspondent at St. Petersburg sends an account of an interview with Father Gopon, whom the correspondent describes as a slender, brown-bearded, mild-eyed man of 50. He is as calm in private as he is fiery on the tribune. In speaking of the plans for tomorrow's demonstration Father Gopon said:

We will meet in the Winter Palace square at 4 o'clock Sunday afternoon. We have notified Prince Mirsky that we desire to meet the emperor at that time and that we expect his majesty to attend and to receive the petition for a constitution. If he refuses there will be terrible uprisings. It is quite possible that the prefect or minister will come and ask us to give him the petition instead of the emperor, but we do not intend to listen to such advice.

Expects 100,000 to Gather.

I expect fully 100,000 inhabitants will gather in the neighborhood of the palace, of whom 100,000 will be working men. Very possibly I may perish on Sunday but am convinced that bloodshed, if it comes, will bring us liberty.

If the emperor is wise he will come to St. Petersburg and meet us. Our immediate demand is for the convocation of a constituent assembly. We do not ask his majesty to discuss the details. If he promises, all will be well; if he refuses or absents himself the consequences will be terrible. God grant that Russia may soon be as free as England.

Will Carry No Red Flags.
The Telegraph correspondent at St. Petersburg also had an interview with Father Gopon in which he said:

We shall come without red flags, without revolutionary hymns or cries, simply as loyal citizens to obtain hearing of his majesty, who has been deceived by bad needs, but will, we trust, learn then from us. If the police or Cossacks bar our way to the palace or try to disperse us as they dispersed the crowd in Moscow, they can employ force and spill blood, and I will continue to stand in front as behooves a leader who is responsible for the fateful action of his trusting comrades, and if the authorities shoot us down, I shall doubtless be first to fall. But our blood will accomplish more than the most successful agitation.

Most St. Petersburg correspondents of the London papers adhere to the theory that the Neva incident was the result of a deliberately planned attempt on the life of the czar.

En un país como el nuestro sobre el cual ha estado amenazando por tanto tiempo una ruina moral material, que solo ha evitado el esfuerzo súbito potente de la mayor parte de sus hijos, es natural que el pueblo muestre cierta desconfianza, a veces injusta, con todos los que le juzgan. Somos de los que creen que hay salud en la crítica; pero también opinamos que al mismo tiempo que se debe desconfiar de lo peor del hombre se ha de tener fe en lo mejor de él. Y lo mejor de Mr. Tyler en este caso es que viene exteriorizando en la prensa americana incidentes vergonzosos de la vida oficial de Puerto Rico; cosa que ningún otro continental pudo hacer bajo el régimen que acalla hasta el poder de censura.

Si bien es verdad que el corresponsal del Harper's incurre en injusticias que han servido de pie a magníficos artículos de esa doctrina en varios voceros, también es cierto que hay mucho que aplaudir y agradecer a este periodista de los más humanos.

La mejor prueba de que nuestra isla no está satisfecha de sus condiciones se encuentra en esta exquisite sensibilidad patriótica que ha despertado en el pecho puertorriqueño una larga serie de provocaciones y parcialidades.

En artículo del Sun, Nueva York, publicado en su edición del 1A del corriente, que a continuación traduzco, viene demostrar la eficacia de toda propaganda, aunque tenga los lunares que, indudablemente, oscurecen la correspondencia de Mr. Tyler al Harper's:

LA AUMENTA LA INQUIETUD EN PUERTO RICO.—En el último de sus artículos sobre Puerto Rico que viene publicando en el Harper's Weekly Mr. Charles W. Tyler, declara que el anti-americanismo en la isla es una "enfermedad creciente". Mr. Charles W. Domenech, líder político que también es director de uno de los pocos periódicos pro-americano que se publican en Puerto Rico, aporta la opinión en el sentido de que no es improbable que el sentimiento anti-americano en la isla culmine en demostraciones de resistencia a aquellas formas rechazables de autoridad en "colisiones físicas de alguna clase" en la región montañesa.

Mr. Tyler encuentra la causa de este general sentimiento en el mismo estado de cosas que nos ha hecho a nosotros usar la frase de "nuestra isla olvidada" por lo que Puerto Rico respecta. Observa tres causas específicas y fundamentales de queja, dice que se remediarán "poco queda de la actual extensa agitación, como si fuera los meros vapores y la espuma de superficie."

Reconoce como causas primordiales de este aumento, primero: la severidad de la situación económica en los distritos cafetaleros; segundo: el presente humillante e indefinido status de los puertorriqueños por lo que se relaciona con su ciudadanía; tercero: "los nombramientos oficiales han sido otorgados basándose más bien en la influencia política que en la capacidad."

Ya hemos aludido nosotros con frecuencia a la severidad del estado económico y a la cuestión de la ciudadanía, pero es absurdo en la presente situación. Nuestros tribunales se niegan a reconocer a los puertorriqueños como ciudadanos de los Estados Unidos. De otra parte no son extranjeros, por esa razón no pueden hacerse ciudadanos por medio de la naturalization. Se encuentran sin patria, habitantes de una isla que es prácticamente una colonia política. Por lo tocante a los nombramientos se han hecho algunos, tal vez muchos, hombres idóneos y valiosos; pero se han otorgado tantos otros de carácter distinto que hacen posible que el corresponsal de una publicación tan acreditada como Harper's Weekly se refiera a ellos en esta forma: "espectáculo forense de borrachos, incapaces y peores, que han sido enviados aquí entre los nombrados desde Washington durante los pasados siete años."

Un esfuerzo se hará para llamar la atención del Congreso hacia los asuntos de Puerto Rico en la próxima sesión. A los puertorriqueños debería ofrecerse atención completamente.

J. COLLAZO y.

Protective Association of Threshermen Agrees on 6 and 9 1-2 Cents Per Bushel.


The Northwestern Threshermen's second meeting at Walla Walla last Saturday afternoon. The first meeting of this association was held at the same place two weeks previous, but at that time nothing of importance was transacted except to appoint committee to draft a constitution and by-laws to govern the future deliberations of the association. The objects for which the association is being formed are primarily to regulate the price of threshing throughout the counties of Umatilla, Walla Walla and Columbia, and also to bring the numerous threshermen together and enable them to become better acquainted with one another.


The association will also fix the territory the different crews will operate in, and in that manner do away with the ruinous practice which has hitherto prevailed, of cutting prices and of two or more outfits working in such close proximity as to entail great loss of time and the consequent expense in moving miles across the country to new location.


As there are nearly 200 large machines costing over $4,000 each in the three counties named, and in some instances they have been threshing for as low as four cents a bushel, it can readily be seen that the benefits to threshermen to accrue from the new association will be immense.

To illustrate what I mean, take the matter of procuring charters from the commission, in the matter the commission acts ministerially—that is, the application, or certificate of incorporation, as the law calls it, embodies the specific requirements of the statute; the commission may be compelled to grant the charter by appeal to the Court of Appeals if it refuses. Dishonest Practices Of Agents, Employes and Servants, and Those Dealing with Them.

PASSED April 11, 1867

It is enacted by the General Assembly as follows:

Section 1. No person shall corruptly give or offer any gift or valuable consideration to any such agent, employe, servant, or public official as an inducement or reward for doing or forbearing to do, or for having done or forborne to do any act in relation to the business of his principal, master, or employer, or the state, city, or town of which he is an official, or for showing or forbearing to show favor or disfavor to any person in relation to the business of his principal, master, employer, or state, city, or town of which he is an official.

and after you've fed the tapeworm
there's mighty little left for you. Fol-
lowing the horses may be pleasant ex-
ercise at the start, but they're apt to
lead you to the door of the poorhouse
or the jail at the finish.

To get back to Clarence, he took
about an hour to dock his cargo of
hard luck and another to tell me how
strange it was that there was no draft
from his London bankers waiting to
welcome him. Naturally I haven't
lived for sixty years among a lot of
fellows who've been trying to drive a
cold chisel between me and my bank
account without being able to smell a
touch coming a long time before it
overtakes me, and Clarence's inten-
tions permeated his cheeky conversa-
tion about as thoroughly as a fertilizer
factory does a warm summer night.

Of course he gave me every opportuni-
ty to prove that I was a gentleman
and to suggest delicately that I should
be glad if he would let me act as his
banker in this sudden emergency, but
as I didn't show any signs of being a
gentleman and banker he was finally
forced to come out and ask me in
coarse commercial words to lend him a
hundred. Said it hurt him to have to
do it on such short acquaintance, but I
couldn't see that he was suffering any
real pain.

ence a dollar on his looks or his story,
for they both struck me as doubtful
collateral, but so long as he had a
letter from you asking me to do any
thing in my power to oblige him or to
make his stay in Carlsbad pleasant,
let him have the money on your ac-
count, to which I have written the
cashier to charge it. Of course I hope
Clarence will pay you back, but think
you will save bookkeeping by charg-
ing it off to experience. I've usually
found that these quick, glad borrowers
are slow, sad payers. And when a fel-
low tells you that it hurts him to
have to borrow you can bet that the
thought of having to pay is going to
tie him up into a bowknot of pain.

Right here I want to caution you
against giving away your signature to
every Clarence and Willie that happens
along. When your name is on a note
it stands only for money, but when
it's on a letter of introduction or rec-
ommendation it stands for your judg-
ment of ability and character, and you
can't call it in at the end of thirty
days, either. Giving a letter of intro-
duction is simply lending your name
with a man as collateral, and if he's
no good you can't have the satisfaction

once and you're discredited. The first thing

note or ham or a man that isn't good.

luncheon and cigars. It's getting so
that a fellow who's almost a stranger
to me doesn't think anything of ask-
ing for a letter of introduction to one
who's a total stranger. You can't explain
plain to these men, because when you
try to let them down easy by tellin'
them that you haven't had any rea-
l opportunity to know what their specia-

with an, "Oh, that's all right—just say
a word and refer to anything you know
about me—"

and give them the letter then unsealed

of one of those letters being presented

EL OBJETIVO DE LA HIGIENE

El objeto tan universalmente usado para el aseo de la dentadura, debe ser desterrado como uno de los peores enemigos de la higiene. El cepillo de dientes es vivienda natural de microbios y se adapta maravillosamente a la trasmisión y propagación en el organismo por medio de sus penetrantes púas.

El cepillo de dientes, dice el doctor Palier, se ha estado usando por largo tiempo, sin que nadie lo sospeche de daño. En este país se le usa tanto como en América, ni hay país en que tanto favorezca la industria de dentaduras postizas como este. El cepillo de dientes es, en opinión del doctor, aliciente poderoso en el origen de muchos males, y el asunto le parece demasiado importante para pasarlo en silencio.

Nadie ignora que la boca es un hormiguero de microbios, y sometiendo al microscopio una gota de saliva se encuentra cargada de bacilos. En la saliva de personas saludables no es raro hallar gérmenes pulmonares, en adición a lo cual puede haber otros microorganismos patogénicos por diversas causas.

El medio de guardarse contra la infección de estos microorganismos es conservar intacta la membrana mucosa; donde ocurra una ruptura superficial, por insignificante que sea, puede haber infección especialmente cuando se halla en estado de resistir menos que de ordinario, como cuando hay hambre, mucha fatiga, etc. Puede asegurarse, cree el doctor Palier, que muchas enfermedades infecciosas se contraen por la boca. Las fiebres inflamatorias de otras partes del cuerpo se deben, naturalmente, a otro origen de infección, pero hasta dolencias infecciosas del sistema, tales como difteria, escarlatina, etc., entran con frecuencia por la acción de la boca.

Si algo hay eternamente cargado de organismos, es el cepillo de dientes; para dejarle aséptico es necesario someterlo a poderosos germicidas químicos y tenerlo hirviendo mucho tiempo, pues hay microbios que resisten todo otro procedimiento. Rara vez nunca se esteriliza el cepillo de dientes, y al sumo, se le pone cascafia caliente, lo que es del todo inadecuado. Luego es, por lo general, de material duro, cuyas púas se meten entre los dientes, rozan las encías y así actúan como inoculadores de microbios. Por cualidad son virulentos, de seguro, viene una enfermedad.

Por ejemplo una epidemia causada por un paciente que tiene difteria puede muy bien haberla entrado en la boca una partícula de la saliva del enfermo. Que use el cepillo de dientes y roce la membrana mucosa y la tendrá inoculada de difteria; y para la boca no sirven los antisépticos, siendo prácticamente imposible esterilizar esta cavidad con tantos escondrijos sinuosos. Los líquidos polvos que generalmente se usan para la dentadura tampoco tienen poder contra los microbios.

Además, el uso del cepillo causa, con frecuencia, irritación y dolores en las encías. El doctor menciona un caso reciente de persona que fue con su dentadura sobre las encías demasiado delicadas cuyo inconveniente desapareció en absoluto tan pronto como la persona dejó de usar el cepillo. Si en este país se sufre más de los dientes que en Europa, es porque aquí se hace más uso del cepillo que en ninguna otra parte del mundo, y si no es porque es tan raro ver personas de mediana edad, hasta jóvenes, con buena dentadura va se ha hecho cosa usual para señoritas de los años mostrar más dientes de lo que abría la boca; las sonrisas etc. las bellas están perdiendo el aspecto angelical de antaño.

Esto no quiere decir que uno se tenga de limpiar la dentadura. Para el caso lo mejor es un poco de algodón como el tamaño de una nuez; se bana en agua, se le pliega, se le ponen los polvos y se le usa entre el índice y el pulgar. Al principio será algo difícil, pero pronto se acostumbrará uno a usarlo. Este método tiene la ventaja de poder usarse seguido del todo fresco cada vez, por su suavidad no roza las encías ni la irrita. Debe tenerse la precaución de lavar las manos y la cara antes de limpiar la boca.

crop of 1904 is bound to be followed by
high grade production this season,

The Spoiled Children of the World.


Burmese children are the spoiled chill
dren OF the world, according to " G..
Scott O'Connar. In his book, The
Silken East" he says that they are
never punished by their parents, who
universally adore them. They grow up
In the open air with all the grace OF
young, unchecked life THE sheer joy
Of life abides in them,0 says he, "and
they seem to live perpetually at play
in the village street, where they play
game of ninepins with the great seeds
Of a jungle creeper; in the monastery
where they lie upon the floor and
scream out their lessons with lusty de-
light; in the river, in which they splash
and plunge before they can walk; at
the play, where they crawl about
among the feet of the prima donna and
the posing kings, and at the pagoda,
where they hold flowers before them
with faces screwed up to gravity, with
laughter pent up behind it. And if there
be any dispute about the good looks Of
their elders there can be none as to the
prettiness Of Burmese children. .
